subject: pe
topicDisplay: Performance Analysis And Performance Development Programme
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Reliability of a fitness test refers to:
options: How closely it predicts competition success
Whether it measures the correct component
Its ability to produce consistent, repeatable results
questions.explain: Reliability is the consistency of a test's results when repeated under the same conditions.

questions.q: Which training method is most specific for developing aerobic endurance in a marathon runner?
options: Short maximal sprints with full recovery
questions.explain: Continuous sub-maximal training over long durations develops the aerobic system needed for marathon performance.

questions.q: Fartlek training is best described as:
options: 'Speed play' varying pace and terrain continuously
questions.explain: Fartlek ('speed play') varies intensity and terrain within a continuous run, training both aerobic and anaerobic systems.

questions.q: The main physiological purpose of an active warm-up before performance is to:
options: Increase muscle temperature and blood flow, improving oxygen delivery and reducing injury risk
questions.explain: A warm-up raises muscle temperature, increases blood flow and enzyme activity and improves oxygen delivery, enhancing performance and reducing injury risk.

questions.q: The Multi-Stage Fitness Test (bleep test) is used as a predictive test of:
questions.explain: The multi-stage fitness test estimates VO2 max, a measure of aerobic capacity.

questions.q: For a fitness test to be valid, it must:
options: Measure the specific component of fitness it claims to measure
Use the most expensive equipment available
Produce the same result when repeated
Be administered by the same tester
questions.explain: Validity refers to whether a test actually measures the fitness component it is intended to assess.

questions.q: An athlete uses the Karvonen formula to set a target heart-rate zone. This formula is based on:
options: Heart rate reserve (max HR minus resting HR)
questions.explain: The Karvonen method calculates target HR from heart rate reserve (HRmax minus HRrest) to individualise training zones.

questions.q: A weightlifter trains with loads of 1-3 reps at near-maximal weight. This rep range primarily develops:
questions.explain: Low repetitions at very high loads (around 90%+ 1RM) target maximal strength via neural and structural adaptations.

questions.q: An active cool-down helps recovery primarily by:
options: Trapping blood in the lower limbs
Maintaining venous return and accelerating removal of metabolic by-products such as lactate
questions.explain: Light continued activity in a cool-down maintains the muscle pump and venous return, helping clear lactate and other by-products and aiding recovery.

questions.q: Blood lactate sampling during a graded exercise test is mainly used to identify:
options: The lactate threshold and appropriate training zones
questions.explain: Lactate testing identifies the lactate threshold (often OBLA at ~4 mmol/L), which is used to set individualised training intensities.

questions.q: The principle of reversibility states that:
options: Fitness gains are lost when training stops or is reduced
Adaptations are gained faster than they are lost
Training must be specific to the activity
questions.explain: Reversibility ('use it or lose it') describes the loss of training adaptations when the stimulus is removed or reduced.

questions.q: Cardiac hypertrophy resulting from prolonged endurance training mainly causes:
options: A thicker but smaller left ventricle
An increased stroke volume and lower resting heart rate (bradycardia)
questions.explain: Endurance training enlarges the left ventricle, increasing stroke volume so the heart pumps more blood per beat and resting heart rate falls.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of QUANTITATIVE performance analysis?
options: Counting the number of successful passes a player completes
A coach's verbal impression of an athlete's effort
questions.explain: Quantitative analysis produces numerical data, such as a count of completed passes, whereas qualitative analysis is descriptive.

questions.q: Plyometric training relies primarily on which mechanism to develop power?
questions.explain: Plyometrics use a rapid eccentric (stretch) phase immediately followed by a concentric contraction, exploiting the stretch-shortening cycle for explosive power.

questions.q: Tapering in the days before a major competition primarily involves:
options: A reduction in training volume while maintaining intensity
A sharp increase in training volume
questions.explain: Tapering reduces training volume to allow recovery and supercompensation while keeping intensity high so fitness is preserved for peaking.

questions.q: Specificity in training design means that:
options: All athletes follow the same generic programme
Fitness is lost when training stops
Training should replicate the movements, energy systems and muscle groups of the activity
questions.explain: The principle of specificity requires training to match the demands of the sport in terms of muscles used, energy systems and movement patterns.

questions.q: Creatine supplementation is most likely to benefit which type of performance?
questions.explain: Creatine increases phosphocreatine stores, supporting the ATP-PC system used in short, explosive, high-intensity efforts.

questions.q: Blood doping (including EPO use) enhances endurance by:
options: Increasing red blood cell mass and oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explain: Blood doping and EPO raise red blood cell/haemoglobin levels, increasing oxygen transport to working muscles, but both are illegal and dangerous.

questions.q: Using analysis to plan performance development, the correct logical sequence is:
options: Set goals, then collect data, then ignore feedback
Implement training, then never review it
Collect objective data, evaluate against a model, set SMART targets, then implement and re-assess
questions.explain: Effective development uses data collection, evaluation against an optimal model, SMART goal-setting, intervention and re-assessment in a continuous cycle.

questions.q: The Wingate test is primarily used to assess:
questions.explain: The 30-second maximal Wingate cycle test measures anaerobic power output and capacity.

questions.q: The principle of progressive overload is best defined as:
options: Gradually increasing the demands placed on the body over time
Training only the muscles specific to the sport
questions.explain: Progressive overload means systematically and gradually increasing training demands so the body continues to adapt.

questions.q: Which of the following is a LEGAL ergogenic aid?
questions.explain: Caffeine is a legal stimulant, whereas anabolic steroids, EPO and blood doping are prohibited.

questions.q: Adequate hydration during prolonged exercise is important mainly because dehydration:
options: Has no measurable effect on performance
Reduces plasma volume, raising heart rate and impairing thermoregulation
questions.explain: Dehydration lowers blood plasma volume, increasing cardiovascular strain and reducing the ability to dissipate heat, which impairs performance.

questions.q: PNF stretching typically improves flexibility by:
options: Contracting the muscle isometrically before relaxing and stretching further
Holding a static position passively only
questions.explain: PNF uses an isometric contraction of the target muscle followed by relaxation, inhibiting the stretch reflex and allowing a greater range of movement.

questions.q: A resistance programme of 3 sets of 12-15 repetitions at a moderate load is designed mainly to develop:
questions.explain: Higher repetitions (around 12-15+) at moderate loads target muscular endurance rather than maximal strength or power.

questions.q: GPS tracking units worn by team-sport athletes most directly provide data on:
options: Distance covered, speed and high-intensity running loads
questions.explain: GPS units quantify locomotor demands such as total distance, velocity, accelerations and high-speed running to monitor external training load.

questions.q: Qualitative analysis of technique differs from quantitative analysis because it:
options: Provides descriptive, subjective judgements of movement quality
questions.explain: Qualitative analysis gives a descriptive, often subjective, evaluation of the quality of a movement rather than a numerical value.

questions.q: The RICE protocol used in the acute management of a soft-tissue injury stands for:
questions.explain: RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) limits swelling and bleeding in the acute phase of a soft-tissue injury.

questions.q: Comparing an athlete's technique against an 'elite model' is valuable because it:
options: Guarantees the athlete will reach elite level
Removes the need for any feedback
Provides an optimal reference template to identify and correct technical faults
questions.explain: An elite or perfect model gives a benchmark of optimal technique against which faults can be identified and corrective feedback given.

questions.q: During the competitive (in-season) phase of periodisation, the focus typically shifts towards:
options: Maintaining fitness, refining skill and peaking for competition
questions.explain: The competition phase prioritises maintenance of fitness, skill refinement and peaking, with reduced volume relative to the preparation phase.
